title: Short Encoding of Words
description: Brute force to optimized: pairwise suffix checks versus suffix removal from a hash set (a reversed-trie equivalent).

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: A valid encoding of an array of words is a reference string s and an array of indices such that for each index, the substring of s starting there up to the next hash mark equals the word (the encoding stores each word followed by a hash mark, and shares suffixes). Return the length of the shortest possible reference string s.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","words array of distinct strings"],["Output","The minimum length of a valid encoding string"],["Key Insight","A word that is a suffix of another word does not need its own separate entry"],["Constraints","Up to 2000 words, each up to 7 characters"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Shared suffixes reduce the encoding\"","Reversing each word turns suffix-sharing into prefix-sharing, a natural trie fit"],["\"Only words that are NOT a suffix of any other word need an entry\"","A reversed trie: a word survives only if its reversed node has no children (nothing extends it further)"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

If word A is a suffix of word B (like "me" is a suffix of "time"), then encoding B alone (as "time#") already covers A, since A appears as the tail of B followed by the hash mark. So only words that are NOT a suffix of any other word need their own entry, each contributing its length plus one (for the hash mark).

blocks.title: Analogy: Keeping Only the Longest Version of Overlapping Nicknames
blocks.text: Picture a list of nicknames where some are just the tail end of others (like "me" being the end of "time"). Keeping only the nicknames that are not merely the ending of some longer one in the list avoids storing redundant shorter entries.

blocks.caption: A word that is a suffix of another word does not need its own entry in the encoding

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: words = ["time", "me", "bell"]
"me" is a suffix of "time", so it is dropped. "time" and "bell" remain, each getting a hash mark: "time#bell#", length 10.
Example: words = ["t"]
Single word "t" needs its own entry: "t#", length 2.
5. How Should We Think?

Before checking every word against every other word for the suffix relationship directly, notice that reversing every word turns "is a suffix of" into "is a prefix of", which is exactly what a trie is built to detect efficiently.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A word needs no entry if some OTHER word ends with it (it is a suffix of that other word).

Observation 2: Reversing each word converts the suffix relationship into a prefix relationship: "me" reversed is "em", and "time" reversed is "emit", and "em" is a prefix of "emit".

Observation 3: Inserting all reversed words into a trie, a word's reversed form is a proper prefix of another's exactly when its trie node still has children after all insertions.

Observation 4: Only reversed words landing on a trie node with NO children (nothing extends past it) represent words that need their own entry; sum their (length plus one) for the answer.
This leads to inserting every reversed word into a trie, then summing (length plus one) only for words whose reversed trie node has no children.
6. Brute Force Solution
For each word, check directly whether it is a suffix of any other word in the list; if so, it does not need its own entry.
Why the code is written this way

items: Directly checking suffix membership pairwise implements the definition simply.
This costs O(n squared times average length), wasteful since a reversed trie detects all suffix relationships in one shared structure.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared times average word length) for pairwise suffix checks.
Space: O(n) for the deduplicated word set.
Limitation: a reversed trie converts every pairwise suffix check into shared prefix structure built once, checked via each word's node having children or not.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Insert every word REVERSED into a trie (or equivalently, remove from a hash set of words every proper suffix of another word by checking word.slice(i) for i from 1 to end). A word contributes to the answer only if it is not a proper suffix of any other word in the set, meaning nothing "extends past" it. Sum (length plus one) over exactly those survivors.
Remove from the word set every proper suffix of every word (equivalent to checking reversed-trie children), then sum (length plus one) over the words that remain.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run

blocks.content: {"headers":["Word","Its proper suffixes removed from the set"],"rows":[["time","ime, me, e"],["me","(already removed as a suffix of time)"],["bell","ell, ll, l"]]}

blocks.text: Remaining in the set: time, bell, each contributing length plus one: 5 + 5 = 10.
Why This Works

Removing every proper suffix of every word from the set leaves exactly the words that are not a suffix of any other word (equivalently, the words whose reversed form has no trie children), each of which must contribute its own hash-mark-terminated entry to the reference string, giving the minimum total length.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(total characters squared) worst case for substring extraction and hashing (or O(total characters) with a true reversed trie).
Space: O(total characters) for the set or trie.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Pairwise suffix check","O(n squared times avg length)","O(n)","Correct, but redundant comparisons."],["Suffix removal via hash set / reversed trie","O(total characters), roughly","O(total characters)","The expected, efficient solution."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Short Encoding of Words is a classic reversed-trie (or suffix-removal) technique: converting a suffix relationship into a prefix relationship makes it trie-friendly.
Common Mistakes

items: Checking suffixes without first deduplicating the word list, causing a word to spuriously remove itself.
Forgetting the plus one for the hash mark when summing surviving word lengths.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["All words are suffixes of one single longest word","Only that one longest word contributes to the encoding."],["No word is a suffix of any other","Every word contributes its own length plus one."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "reversing the words turns this suffix problem into a prefix problem, which a trie naturally solves" demonstrates the key transformation insight.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "share suffixes to minimize a combined representation", think: reverse the strings and use a trie (or suffix removal via a hash set) to find prefix relationships.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you reconstruct the actual encoding string and index array, not just its length?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Replace Words and Longest Word in Dictionary, other trie-based dictionary problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The pairwise suffix check approach costs O(n squared times average length); the suffix-removal (reversed trie) approach costs roughly O(total characters), the standard efficient solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: reverse suffix relationships into prefix relationships via a trie (or equivalent suffix removal from a hash set).
Core Idea: a word needs no entry if it is a proper suffix of another word in the list.
Time: O(n squared times average length) for the brute force, roughly O(total characters) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: reversing words turns this into a familiar prefix-sharing problem.
Interview Difficulty: a clean medium-level trie/suffix problem.
One line memory trick: reverse it, then it is just prefixes.
